name: Holikachuk
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.verdict: a source was named but could not be reached
earlier_scan.source_named: Kari, James. 1978. Holikachuk Noun Dictionary (Preliminary). Alaska Native Language Center. 63 pp. (GlottologGlottolog's fullest description is a phonology or text collection)
earlier_scan.note: ANLA archive holding, not readable online; least-documented Alaska Native language per Wikipedia.

sources.citation: Kari, James, with Jimmy Alexander, Olga Deacon, John Deacon. 1976 (rev. March 1978). Holikachuk Literacy Exercises; Holikachuk Months; Holikachuk Bird Names. ANLC typescript with drafts and ms. notes on vowels. ANLA HO975K1976a, 105 scanned pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Alphabet chart and 40 key-word lists by letter, month and bird names, plus drafts; scanned of all 105 pages finds no 'stress', 'accent', 'tone' or 'pitch' (only 'pitch' = spruce gum).

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1974. [Holikachuk alphabet.] Ms. ditto, consonant and vowel charts with key words, 3 pp. ANLA HO974L1974b.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Alphabet chart and key words only; no stress or tone marks or remarks.

sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 1962. [Holikachuk notes, 1962.] Ms. fieldnotes from Mrs. Dementieff (McGrath) and Billy King (Anchorage, 22-23 July 1962); first documentation of Holikachuk as a distinct language. ANLA HO962K1962, 16 scanned pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Handwritten; pp. 1-3 viewed: consonant inventory, *ts > tth, loss of final clusters, vowels 'same as Koyukon'; no stress or tone remark seen. Remaining pages not read.

sources.citation: Oliverio, Giulia R. M. 2004. Holikachuk Athabaskan Phonology. Draft typescript (8 pp. draft grammar, 2 pp. Pronunciation Guide, 5 pp. Holikachuk Literacy, 1 p. notes), annotated by M. Krauss. ANLA HO000O2004. Marked 'DRAFT!!! Do not cite without permission.'
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing. Sections 1.1 consonants and 1.2 vowels only; the draft ends at the vowel chart on typed p. 8 ('Holikachuk has six vowels. Four are long vowels, phonetically long and tense, and two short vowels, phonetically short and lax.'); Krauss's marginal note: 'Too bad this stops here'. Pronunciation guide and literacy sheets list vowels/consonants with key words; no stress, accent or tone anywhere (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent + visual check of the vowel page).
Consonant and vowel tables only; no statement on stress, tone or accent. Cites Kari 1978 (ANLA PDF) and Krauss 2005.

sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 2005. Recognizing Holikachuk as a Distinct Language: A History, 1834-1981. Ms., June 2005 (three drafts plus photocopied sources). ANLA HO962K2005, 168 scanned pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Ms. p. 4 (scan p. 4; same text on scan pp. 8 and 22): the possible survival of traces of low-marked tone in Holikachuk is 'one major question still remaining even for the basic phonology'; no transcription by Krauss, Leer or Kari was made with regard to tone; Zimmerman's 1959 transcriptions carry numerical tone marks; Krauss recalls -ta- in notàtheyo 'he went back' 'seemed not to rise' from a 2004 phone test with Elizabeth Keating.

sources.citation: Cook, Eung-Do & Keren Rice (eds.). 1989. Athapaskan Linguistics: Current Perspectives on a Language Family. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Holikachuk appears only in lists of Alaskan languages (prefix absence, suffix -o); no Holikachuk stress statement.

sources.citation: Krauss, M. E. 1981. Yazyki korennogo naseleniya Alyaski: proshloe, nastoyashchee i budushchee. In Traditsionnye kul'tury Severnoi Sibiri i Severnoi Ameriki, 149-181. Moscow: Nauka. (Russian version of Krauss 1980, ANLC Research Papers 4.) Photocopy of pp. 149, 168-169 inside Krauss 2005 (scan pp. 140-141).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Holikachuk paragraph p. 168 is sociolinguistic (recognised in the 1960s, ~160 people, intermediate between Ingalik and Koyukon, Kari's 1974-78 work); nothing on stress or tone.

sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. & Victor Golla. 1981. Northern Athapaskan Languages. In June Helm (ed.), Handbook of North American Indians 6: Subarctic, 67-85. Washington: Smithsonian. Pages 70 and 74 only, photocopied inside Krauss 2005 (scan pp. 142-143).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Holikachuk paragraph (p. 74) gives only consonant/vowel isoglosses vs Koyukon (PA *c > theta-series, no stem-final clusters, prefixal *e/*a merge) and speaker numbers; nothing on stress or tone. Fig. 1d 'Development of tone systems' (p. 70) shows Ho (Holikachuk) in the unshaded class 'Tone system absent or vestigial'. Full chapter (pp. 67-85) not opened.

sources.citation: Kari, James (comp.), with Jimmy Alexander, John Deacon, Olga Deacon. 1978. Holikachuk Noun Dictionary (Preliminary). Fairbanks: Alaska Native Language Center. iii+58 pp. (ERIC ED172528).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Introduction (pp. i-iii) gives the consonant chart, compares consonants with Koyukon and Deg Hit'an, the six-vowel system and prefix-vowel neutralisation; no mention of stress, accent, tone or pitch; the practical orthography marks no prominence.

sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 2005. Athabaskan tone. In Sharon Hargus & Keren Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 269), 55-136. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. (Written 1979.)
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: publisher record (DOI); no open copy and no library e-access found (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Family-wide comparative survey of tone that classifies each language; expected to list Holikachuk among the toneless/vestigial Alaskan languages.

sources.citation: Oliverio, Giulia R. M. (interviewer) & Wilson Deacon (speaker). 2001. [Holikachuk field recordings with Wilson Deacon.] 15 digital audio recordings, mainly verb paradigms, 27 March - 15 June 2001. ANLA HO000O2001b.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Best-quality audio of a fluent speaker; an instrumental check of prominence (duration/F0) would be the only route to a stress statement now that the language is dormant. No online files listed by the ANLA file API.

sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 1979. Na-Dene and Eskimo-Aleut. In Lyle Campbell & Marianne Mithun (eds.), The Languages of Native America, 803-901. Austin: University of Texas Press (Holikachuk pp. 852-853).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Comparative/historical survey; Krauss 2005 cites it as one of his published comments on Holikachuk; likely sociolinguistic only, but not seen.

sources.citation: Kari, James. 1975-1978. Ingalik/Holikachuk field notebooks #1, #4; Holikachuk notes 1977-1978. ANLA IK974K1975b, IK974K1977, HO975K1977a.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: open copy online, not downloaded; the open copy was too large to download
sources.note: Kari's raw transcriptions may carry occasional stress or length marks; open scans at ANLA but handwritten and long, not read.

sources.citation: Zimmerman, Herbert. 1959. SIL questionnaire transcriptions from Shageluk-Holikachuk speakers (mixed Holikachuk and Ingalik material), 'with numerical tone-markings throughout' per Krauss 2005:4.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only known Holikachuk record with pitch/tone marked on every word; Krauss names it as the place to check for vestigial tone; would be the raw material for any prominence statement.
